content: Rotavirus infection is the leading cause of severe diarrhea in children and is a significant contributor to gastroenteritis. Vaccination against rotavirus is crucial to prevent future infections. The virus is primarily transmitted via the fecal-oral route and spreads through viral replication. It is essential to distinguish rotavirus infections from other causes of watery diarrhea, such as adenovirus, Escherichia coli, and Taenia species. Children, particularly those in childcare centers or those who are unvaccinated, are at higher risk of infection. Clinical symptoms include diarrhea, vomiting, and low-grade fever. In severe cases, dehydration may occur, with signs such as sunken eyes and pallor. Rotavirus was first identified in 1973 by Dr. Ruth Bishop after years of research into unexplained cases of gastroenteritis in children. The infection can be categorized based on age into adult and child rotavirus infections, though no formal classification system exists. The virus is transmitted through the fecal-oral route, often via contaminated hands, food, or objects like toys. Viral replication occurs in the intestine, leading to the destruction of digestive enzymes and malabsorption, which results in severe watery diarrhea. Rotavirus protein number 4 plays a critical role in the pathogenesis and clinical manifestations of the disease. Although primarily an intestinal infection, rotavirus can also affect the central nervous system, potentially causing meningitis. Rotaviruses belong to the Reoviridae family, with seven major groups identified. Groups A, B, and C infect humans, with group A being the most prevalent. Rotavirus is the most common cause of severe diarrhea in children, responsible for approximately 600,000 deaths annually in developing countries as of 2005. Differentiating rotavirus from other causes of watery diarrhea is essential. It must be distinguished from infections caused by adenovirus, Escherichia coli, and Taenia species. Rotavirus is the leading cause of severe diarrhea in infants and children, affecting around 120 million individuals annually and causing 600,000–650,000 deaths worldwide. The infection is more common in winter, in children rather than adults, and in developing countries. There is no racial predilection. Children in childcare centers and unvaccinated children are at higher risk of rotavirus infection. Immunocompromised individuals and adults in close contact with infected children are also at risk. Rotavirus infection is typically self-limiting but can lead to complications such as dehydration and, in rare cases, seizures. Dehydration is the most significant complication. The prognosis for rotavirus infection is generally favorable. Symptoms are more severe in children than in adults, with the first infection being the most severe. Symptoms range from asymptomatic cases to severe watery diarrhea and dehydration. Infected children may present with high-grade fever and vomiting. Convulsions may occur in severe cases. Diagnosis of rotavirus infection involves various techniques, including electron microscopy, reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), and RNA electrophoresis. Stool examination is crucial for detecting the virus. Antigen detection can be performed using ELISA and immunochromatographic assays. Imaging studies, such as X-rays, CT scans, and ultrasounds, do not show specific findings for rotavirus infection but may be used to rule out other conditions. The cornerstone of treatment for rotavirus infection is preventing dehydration. This should begin at home, with the use of oral rehydration solutions (ORS) as recommended by the CDC. Families with young children are advised to keep a supply of ORS at home and administer it at the onset of diarrhea. Medications, including antibiotics, are not effective against viruses and should only be used if specifically recommended by a physician. Surgical intervention is not indicated for rotavirus infection. Prevention of rotavirus infection relies heavily on vaccination. Two vaccines, Rotarix and RotaTeq, were introduced in 2006 and have been shown to be safe and effective.
